title: Discovery of connectivity-trainability trade-off of IQP Circuits for Hamiltonian Optimization
abstract: Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits are promising candidates for near-term quantum advantage due to the conjectured classical hardness of their sampling task. However, their capabilities for optimization remain largely unexplored. We present a systematic investigation of the performance and trainability of IQP circuits for Hamiltonian optimization. Our results reveal a trade-off between optimization performance and circuit connectivity, demonstrating that the circuit structure plays a key role in determining the ability of IQP circuits to reach low-energy states.
summary: This paper analyzes how the connectivity structure of IQP quantum circuits affects their ability to solve complex Hamiltonian optimization problems. It establishes a crucial trade-off: highly expressive, fully connected circuits are prone to vanishing gradients (barren plateaus), while less expressive but stable circuits perform poorly. The authors conclude that an intermediate connectivity, like circular coupling, offers the most robust balance for near-term quantum computation.
main_problem: The study investigates the fundamental trade-off between optimization performance (expressivity) and training stability (trainability) when using Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits for solving Hamiltonian optimization problems.
main_result: A clear trade-off exists: fully connected circuits offer high expressivity but suffer from rapid gradient decay (barren plateaus), while single-Z circuits are stable but under-expressive; circular connectivity provides the best balance.
method: The authors systematically compared three IQP circuit architectures (single-Z, circular, full) by minimizing expectation values of benchmark Hamiltonians and analyzing gradient variance scaling with system size.
model_or_system: The model uses IQP circuits as variational ansätze to approximate the ground state energy of various combinatorial Hamiltonians, such as Ising or MaxCut models. The analysis focuses on how circuit connectivity dictates the optimization landscape's properties.
key_observables: Relative approximation ratio (optimization performance), gradient variance decay rate (trainability/barren plateau susceptibility), expressibility (Jensen-Shannon distance), and bipartite entanglement entropy.
important_parameters: Circuit connectivity structure (Single-Z, Circular, Full); System size (number of qubits $n$); Optimization parameters ($	heta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the trade-off between expressivity and trainability is a fundamental constraint for near-term quantum advantage in optimization tasks.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how connectivity affects expressibility (approaching Haar-random behavior) and entanglement entropy, while gradient variance plots show full connectivity decaying fastest, indicating barren plateaus.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces IQP circuits for Hamiltonian optimization, analyzes performance metrics across different connectivities using benchmark Hamiltonians, and concludes by mapping out the necessary balance between expressivity and trainability required for practical quantum algorithms.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms—the conflict between achieving high representational power (expressivity) and maintaining gradients that allow for efficient classical optimization (trainability).

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Structure of an IQP circuit. The circuit begins with Hadamard gates that prepare a uniform superposition, followed by a diagonal unitary D(θ) = exp  i P j θjZgj  , where Zgj is a tensor product of Pauli-Z operators acting on the qubits indicated by the bitstring gj ∈{0, 1}n. The computation is completed by a second layer of Hadamard gates and measurement in the computational basis.

Fig. 2: Comparison of the optimization error achieved by IQP circuits for different Hamiltonians and parameter initialization strategies. The relative approximation ratio is shown as a function of the number of qubits for the classical Ising Model, MaxCut, and Number Partition Hamiltonians. Results are obtained using 1000 optimization iterations, 50 randomly generated problem instances, and 1000 Monte Carlo samples per configuration. Fully connected IQP circuits generally achieve lower relative approximation ratios than circular and single-Z architectures, while the π/4 initialization provides the oscillated performance across different problem instances.

Fig. 3: Gradient variance as a function of the number of qubits with the same setup as in Fig. 2. When increasing the system size, fully connected circuits exhibit a faster decay of gradient variance than circular and single-Z architectures, indicating a stronger tendency toward barren plateaus. Conversely, sparse circuit structures maintain larger gradients and improved trainability, revealing a trade-off between circuit expressivity and optimization landscape.

Fig. 2 compares the optimization performance of IQP cir- cuits with different connectivity structures on the three bench- mark Hamiltonians. Across all initialization strategies and problem classes, fully connected circuits generally achieve the smallest relative approximation ratios, indicating their superior ability to approximate the ground-state energy. Circular archi- tectures provide intermediate performance, whereas single-Z circuits consistently exhibit larger optimization errors. This trend becomes more pronounced for the Number Partition Hamiltonian, whose dense interaction structure requires the circuit to capture long-range correlations among qubits. The plots compare IQP circuits with full connectivity, circular connectivity, and single-Z terms in terms of expressibility (Fig. 4a) and average bipartite entanglement entropy (Fig. 4b) as a function of the number of qubits.
